sections.html:
Bensalem is a township of about 62,800 people at the southern tip of Bucks County, up against the Northeast section of Philadelphia. Population is 62,783 for July 1, 2025, up slightly from 62,707 in the 2020 census, and it is the most populous municipality in the county. Despite the word township, it has had a mayor and a five-member council since voters chose that form in 1987. There are no boroughs inside its lines. Andalusia, Cornwells Heights, Eddington, Oakford and Trevose are communities within the one township, and each shows up in mailing addresses and listings, so a house with a Trevose address is still a Bensalem Township property for permits and taxes.

Homeownership runs at 62.3 percent for 2020 to 2024, and the median home value is $364,400. Treat that as a township-wide survey estimate, not a price for your address.

Households here are mostly owners, and the numbers below give a rough picture of who is buying and what they carry.

sections.h2: What a Bensalem seller must file before closing
sections.html:
Bensalem requires a Residential Resales Use and Occupancy permit whenever a dwelling changes hands. The Building and Planning Department's application form describes it as the permit to occupy a single or multi-family dwelling or condominium through new ownership or new use. The fee is $100.

  • File the application one month before the settlement date. The form is signed, and a signed copy is required before the permit issues.
  • Attach an electrical panel certificate from one of the approved electrical underwriters named on the form.
  • Attach a maintenance certificate from a registered contractor saying the heating system is in good working condition.
  • Attach a chimney, flue and vent inspection at NFPA 211 Level II, usually done with a camera.
  • Pay in cash, check or money order. The township does not accept credit cards or electronic payments.

The certifications may be obtained up to one year before settlement, so you can order them early and have them in hand when a buyer appears. Staff search the property's history for open permits, complaints and liens. Unresolved items delay the certificate, and clearing them falls to the seller.

Questions go to the Building and Planning Department at 2400 Byberry Road, phone 215-633-3644, open 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. on weekdays. The township posts its resale application on its website.

The application asks for a settlement date and certificates from outside contractors, so the order of steps matters. Once you have a signed agreement of sale and a closing date, count back one month for the filing. Book the electrician, the heating contractor and the chimney inspector before that, because their certificates have to be attached.

If you are selling for cash on a short timeline, the same rule applies, since the permit follows the change in ownership no matter how the buyer pays. Ordering the three inspections the day you decide to sell is the simplest way to keep a closing date from slipping.

sections.h2: How Bucks County assesses a Bensalem house
sections.html:
The Bucks County Board of Assessment Appeals, at 55 East Court Street in Doylestown, keeps the assessment rolls for Bensalem. Its office number is 215-348-6219, and the board meets at 10 a.m. on the first and third Tuesday of each month.

Annual appeals are due each August, and a change from an annual appeal takes effect the following tax year. Call the board for the current year's date. Homestead and farmstead applications are due by March 1 for the tax year that starts July 1 of that year.

Act 29 also applies when you sell: a new owner must give the Board of Assessment contact information within 30 days of buying a property. Mention that to your buyer so it does not get missed after closing.

sections.h2: What happens if the township finds open items?
sections.html:
When staff search a property's history, they look for open permits, complaints and liens. If something turns up, the certificate waits until it is cleared. A permit left open by a previous owner, a deck built without sign-off or an old complaint can all stall a closing that is otherwise ready.

Walk through the house and the paperwork before you list. Pull any permits you remember pulling, note any work a past owner did, and call the Building and Planning Department if you are unsure. Sorting it out before a buyer is under contract gives you room to fix it on your own schedule instead of the buyer's.

1. Decide how you will sell and set a rough closing date.
  2. Order the electrical panel certificate, the heating maintenance certificate and the chimney inspection. They can be dated up to one year before settlement.
  3. Sign an agreement of sale with a settlement date.
  4. File the signed application and the $100 fee at least one month before settlement.
  5. Clear anything the township flags in its search of permits, complaints and liens.
  6. Call the water, sewer and electric companies with the closing date.
  7. Close, and remind the buyer about the Act 29 contact notice owed to the county within 30 days.

Bensalem's sewer service comes from the Bucks County Water and Sewer Authority and its water from Aqua Pennsylvania, since the township sold both systems in 1999. Utility transfers at closing go through those companies. PECO supplies electricity and natural gas.

Call each provider with the settlement date so final readings and the buyer's start of service line up with the deed.

Houses near Poquessing Creek, Neshaminy Creek or the Delaware River are worth checking for drainage and basement moisture before you list. July is the wettest month, and thunderstorms peak then. A buyer can ask the township's engineering and building staff about the flood zone for a specific parcel, so know the answer for your own lot before the buyer's inspector raises it.

sections.h2: Ways to sell a house fast in Bensalem
sections.html:
A Bensalem owner can list the house, sell directly, or take a cash offer. A listing exposes the house to the most buyers, while a cash purchase removes the lender's appraisal and underwriting from the schedule.

All three routes depend on the same township paperwork. Order the electrical, heating and chimney inspections as soon as a buyer is lined up, and pick a closing date that leaves the one month filing window. Whoever buys, ask for proof of funds, the closing date and who pays for title work in writing.

faqs.q: Does Bensalem require a certificate when a house is sold?
faqs.a: Yes. The township issues a Residential Resales Use and Occupancy permit for a change in ownership, based on electrical, heating and chimney certificates and a $100 application fee.

faqs.q: How far ahead should I apply for the Bensalem resale permit?
faqs.a: About one month before the settlement date. The township asks for the signed application and all three certifications at that point, and it accepts only cash, check or money order.

faqs.q: Who inspects the chimney for a Bensalem sale?
faqs.a: A chimney sweep company of your choice, with an NFPA 211 Level II inspection noted on the certification. The application form also names two companies whose certifications the township will not accept.

faqs.q: Where do I send a Bucks County assessment appeal?
faqs.a: To the Board of Assessment Appeals at 55 East Court Street, 6th floor, Doylestown. Call 215-348-6219 for the current annual filing date.

faqs.q: What do new owners of Bensalem property file with the county?
faqs.a: Under Act 29, a new owner submits contact information to the Board of Assessment within 30 days of the purchase.
